claims.text: Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on a reduced set of ab initio calculations can rapidly and accurately evaluate fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties across elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The proposed training calculations explicitly incorporate anharmonic lattice vibrations and electron-vibration coupling.
A limited set of short ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations can provide training data that reliably capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling.
Actively learned moment-tensor potentials parameterized with ab initio data have been used efficiently in finite-temperature refractory multi-principal-element-alloy workflows.
Near the melting point, the target systems include both solid and liquid configurations relevant to phase coexistence.
Accurately reproducing local atomic environments and free-energy landscapes is the structural mediator controlling solid-liquid phase equilibrium.
The limited ab initio training set will encode the essential temperature-dependent anharmonic and electron-coupling behavior.
The machine-learned potential will interpolate the encoded behavior over a broader configuration space.
The interpolation will drastically reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The machine-learned model will preserve the thermodynamic fidelity needed for solid and liquid free energies.
Predicted phase free energies, fusion temperatures, and specific-heat curves will have fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational expense by approximately an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
The cost advantage will be particularly large for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD are accurate but computationally prohibitive for high-entropy and multicomponent systems.
The method is expected to work near fusion for systems ranging from binary alloys to complex high-entropy alloys.
Performance in systems with extreme chemical ordering or very low symmetry is uncertain.

The hypothesis can be tested by comparing solid and liquid free-energy curves, free-energy crossing temperatures, heat capacities, and entropy contributions against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
A relative deviation exceeding 5–10% in free-energy differences or derived observables, or failure to capture the specified coupling effects, will falsify the hypothesis.
